prompt.context: This is a wild-card / creativity question with no business context. The interviewer wants to see how broadly and creatively you can think under pressure.
prompt.question: Tell me all the ways, practical or not, which you could use to determine whether the light goes off in a refrigerator when you close the door.

framework: Generate ideas across multiple categories: direct mechanical/electrical tests, indirect physical measurements, manufacturing/production-line tests, third-party/information sources, and philosophical/conceptual angles
Aim for breadth over depth — the interviewer is testing creative range, not one correct answer
After ~5 solid answers performance is typically deemed adequate; continue pushing for creativity

brainstorming.prompt: List every way — practical or impractical — to determine whether the refrigerator light turns off when the door is closed.

categories.name: Direct mechanical / electrical tests
ideas: With the door open, press the door button that simulates the door being closed and observe whether the light turns off
Hook wires to the bulb socket and measure current or voltage when the door is physically closed

categories.name: Physical / scientific measurements
ideas: Place a sensitive thermometer (pre-chilled to refrigerator temperature) near the bulb and close the door — a temperature rise indicates the light stayed on
Place light-sensitive photographic film or photochromic material inside and check for exposure after closing the door

categories.name: Durability / statistical tests
ideas: Find the mean time to failure (MTTF) for the bulb, close the door for that duration, then open it and check whether the bulb has burned out — if it has, the light was on
Go to the production line and run a statistically valid sample test by pressing the button mechanism on multiple units to verify the switch cuts power reliably

categories.name: Structural modification
ideas: Drill a small hole in the refrigerator door so you can see (or pass a fiber optic cable through) to observe the interior when the door is closed

categories.name: Information / third-party sources
ideas: Call the manufacturer and ask whether the light is designed to go off when the door closes
Consult the product specification sheet or engineering drawings for the door-switch design

categories.name: Philosophical / conceptual
ideas: If no one is inside the refrigerator to observe the light, does it matter whether it is on? (the philosophical 'tree falls in the forest' angle — acknowledged as highly creative by the interviewer)

recommendation: There is no single correct answer; the goal is to demonstrate breadth, creativity, and comfort with ambiguity
A strong candidate produces 5+ distinct methods spanning at least 3 different categories before pausing
Embrace unconventional angles (philosophical, humorous) alongside practical ones — they signal intellectual range
risks: Fixating on only one category of solutions (e.g., only electrical tests) shows narrow thinking
Long silent pauses without verbalization hurt the impression — narrate your thought process aloud
Over-engineering one solution instead of generating multiple ideas misses the point of the question
next_steps: After delivering ~5 answers, ask the interviewer if they want more or wish to explore any idea further
Reflect on whether ideas span mechanical, physical, informational, and conceptual domains
